Three over-corrections from the previous rounds of this PR, each reproduced at
runtime on 8c3a3ae before being fixed and each anchored on git 2.54.0 run as an
oracle rather than on its documentation.

commondir read through os.Stat, not os.Lstat. git reads `commondir` through the
ordinary stdio path, so it follows a symlink; requiring a regular file by lstat
called a real linked worktree's administrative git directory ordinary content
and left its config and hooks indexable.

    $ ln -s ../realcommondir adm/commondir
    $ git --git-dir=adm rev-parse --git-dir
    adm

A `gitdir:` pointer's target is excluded only when it carries a git directory's
structure. git resolves a `.git` file and then asks is_git_directory() of what
it names, so `gitdir: ../src` naming an ordinary package is `fatal: not a git
repository` to git — and excluding on the pointer alone let any file named
`.git` delete an arbitrary source tree from the index. hasGitDirStructure is
is_git_directory() with only the HEAD test dropped, because the pointer rule
exists precisely to carry a git directory whose HEAD is missing or corrupt,
which is the state that makes git refuse the worktree and the fallback run.

The unlisted-directory sweep asks git which directories it lists nothing under
instead of deriving them. `git ls-files --cached --others --exclude-standard
--directory` reports a pointer-only directory as `nested/` and says nothing
about an ignored `build/`. Deriving them — queueing every ancestor of every
listed path — made the successful git-listing path traverse the whole tree a
second time, ignored build and cache trees included: on a 5,946-directory
fixture whose 501 listed source files sit beside ignored build/ and .cache/
trees, one cold `search` went 0.12 s (origin/main) -> 0.43-0.68 s (8c3a3ae) ->
0.14 s here.

Both directions are pinned. The PR's own reproduction still comes back clean on
every leak shape, and the fixtures that isolate the pointer rule now carry the
objects/ and refs/ that `git init` creates in every real git directory.","messageHeadline":"fix(sem): match git on a symlinked commondir, on a gitfile's target, …","oid":"e5e0748b52bf5114df31adbf98f34e5a86ad0dc5"},{"authoredDate":"2026-08-19T22:00:30Z","authors":[{"email":"257360244+suhaanthayyil@users.noreply.github.com","id":"U_kgDOD1cBdA","login":"suhaanthayyil","name":"Suhaan Thayyil"}],"committedDate":"2026-08-22T09:47:39Z","messageBody":"…g it

`gitdir: admin-link` with `admin-link -> .real-git` recorded only the link's
own spelling, so `.real-git/config` stayed indexable and its remote credential
came back as a ranked search snippet. Git resolves the target with
real_pathdup() — read_gitfile_gently() ends there — so `git rev-parse --git-dir`
answers `.real-git`, and `git ls-files --others --directory` hands `.real-git/`
to the listing as ordinary untracked content. Neither the git listing nor the
filesystem walk descends a symlink, so nothing is ever listed under the link.

The structural rule cannot rescue that directory: the pointer rule exists for a
target whose HEAD is missing or corrupt, which is the state that makes git
refuse the worktree and the filesystem fallback run.

addTarget is the sink for both producers, and already records a git directory
under every spelling the filesystem accepts for it — case folding was the first
such spelling, a symlink is the second. Both spellings are kept, and a target
that resolves outside the repository adds nothing: containment is tested on the
RESOLVED path, since filepath.Join cleans `..` lexically before any link
resolves.","messageHeadline":"fix(sem): resolve a gitfile's target through symlinks before recordin…","oid":"ae86279297879026ee8b043929dd3ced2ff8e3c7"},{"authoredDate":"2026-08-19T22:04:19Z","authors":[{"email":"257360244+suhaanthayyil@users.noreply.github.com","id":"U_kgDOD1cBdA","login":"suhaanthayyil","name":"Suhaan Thayyil"}],"committedDate":"2026-08-22T09:47:39Z","messageBody":"`.git` linked to an in-worktree directory is the third spelling of "the git
directory is not called `.git`", and neither other rule reached it: there is no
`gitdir:` line to parse, and the `.git` component match covers only the link,
which no listing descends. Verified on git 2.54.0 — after
`git init --separate-git-dir=.real-git .` and `ln -s .real-git .git`,
`git rev-parse --git-dir` answers `.git`, so reading `.git/config` reads
`.real-git/config`.

With `.real-git/HEAD` moved aside git says `fatal: not a git repository`, the
filesystem fallback runs, and the structural rule cannot classify a HEAD-less
directory: `.real-git/config` and its remote credential came back as a ranked
search snippet.

observe now asks gitDirLinkTarget alongside gitDirPointerTarget, under the same
structure test the pointer rule applies — git calls `.git` linked to an ordinary
package `not a git repository`, and naming it must not delete that package from
the index.","messageHeadline":"fix(sem): exclude the git directory a `.git` SYMLINK resolves to","oid":"bfe2bdd730b103cdc12e6bada42dc48b62c6854f"},{"authoredDate":"2026-08-19T22:27:58Z","authors":[{"email":"257360244+suhaanthayyil@users.noreply.github.com","id":"U_kgDOD1cBdA","login":"suhaanthayyil","name":"Suhaan Thayyil"}],"committedDate":"2026-08-22T09:47:39Z","messageBody":"`gitCommonDir` decided presence with `os.Stat`, which reports a DANGLING
`commondir` symlink as ENOENT — indistinguishable from no file at all. Git
decides presence with lstat (`file_exists()`), then reads and dies if the read
fails, so it refuses the whole git directory. Verified on git 2.54.0:

    $ ln -s /nonexistent/nowhere adm/commondir
    $ git --git-dir=adm rev-parse --git-dir
    fatal: failed to read adm/commondir: No such file or directory   (exit 128)
    $ rm adm/commondir; git --git-dir=adm rev-parse --git-dir
    adm

Collapsing the two made a fixture tree that merely carries HEAD, objects/ and
refs/ beside a broken `commondir` a git directory, and dropped every file under
it. Failing first on e98d4fc:

    --- FAIL: TestLooksLikeGitDirRejectsCommondirGitRefusesToRead/dangling_symlink
        looksLikeGitDir = true, want false
    --- FAIL: TestSearchRepositoryStillIndexesSourceUnderACommondirGitRefuses
        search did not return testdata/parser/app.go; results = []

Presence is now lstat and the read is still stat, so a symlinked `commondir`
git follows is still followed.

The two rules then part on what a refused `commondir` means, and they must:

- `looksLikeGitDir` refuses the directory, as git does. Nothing but the
  structure claims it is a repository, and git says it is not one.
- `hasGitDirStructure` — the POINTER rule — falls back to the directory itself.
  A `commondir` git will not read is the same damage as the missing HEAD this
  rule already carries: git refuses the repository, which is what makes the
  filesystem fallback run, while the config keeps the credential.

That second half also closes a live under-exclusion, not just a hypothetical:
an empty or directory `commondir` already returned "not a git directory" and so
left a pointer target's credentialed config indexable. Failing first on e98d4fc:

    --- FAIL: TestGitDirExcluderStillExcludesAPointerTargetWhoseCommondirGitRefuses/directory
        excluded(".dead-git/config") = false, want true
    --- FAIL: .../empty
        excluded(".dead-git/config") = false, want true

Both directions are pinned: three shapes git refuses stay indexable under the
standalone rule and excluded under the pointer rule, and the symlinked
`commondir` git accepts is still resolved.","messageHeadline":"fix(sem): tell an absent `commondir` from one git refuses to read","oid":"2da6ace5584647ae73737b8ac0f640bb1eeefebd"},{"authoredDate":"2026-08-19T22:47:24Z","authors":[{"email":"257360244+suhaanthayyil@users.noreply.github.com","id":"U_kgDOD1cBdA","login":"suhaanthayyil","name":"Suhaan Thayyil"}],"committedDate":"2026-08-22T09:47:39Z","messageBody":"`git ls-files --directory` reports an untracked directory as ONE entry no
matter what it holds, so `pkg/` holding `source.go` beside `nested/.git` is
reported as `pkg/` alone while the ordinary listing reports `pkg/source.go`.
The sweep skipped any root already in `seen`, and the ordinary listing had put
`pkg` there — so the pointer-only directory inside it, which appears in neither
listing, was never read and its `--separate-git-dir` target's credentialed
config stayed indexable. Git collapses at the top-most untracked directory, so
the same hole existed at any depth (`pkg/` for `pkg/a/nested/`).

`seen` now guards observation only; a new `queued` set guards the descent, so a
root and its descendants are swept whether or not the listing mentioned content
under them. Only entries ending in `/` become roots: the same listing names
every file and every gitlink without a slash, and those are already observed
through their own chains, so the sweep no longer pays a failed ReadDir per file
in the repository (`directoriesRead` 9 -> 1 in the cost test).","messageHeadline":"fix(sem): sweep inside a directory git's `--directory` listing collapsed","oid":"2b39d6ac4d5b00f48bf9560ab0bcecc525bc8559"},{"authoredDate":"2026-08-19T23:05:01Z","authors":[{"email":"suhaanthayyil0@gmail.com","id":"U_kgDOD1cBdA","login":"suhaanthayyil","name":"Suhaan Thayyil"}],"committedDate":"2026-08-22T09:48:10Z","messageBody":"… trees for pointers

Two more spellings of "a git directory gets indexed as source", both reproduced
at run time on `e00e674` and both settled against git 2.54.0.

`.git` as a SYMLINK to a regular gitfile. Git's read_gitfile_gently() stats the
path and asks S_ISREG of the result, so the link IS a gitfile to git:

    $ ls -l .git realpointer
    lrwxr-xr-x  .git -> realpointer
    -rw-r--r--  realpointer          # gitdir: /…/wt/.real-git
    $ git rev-parse --git-dir
    /…/wt/.real-git
    $ git status --porcelain
    ?? .real-git/

gitDirPointerTarget lstat'd it and required a regular file, so the link was
refused; gitDirLinkTarget accepts only a link to a DIRECTORY; and with the
target's HEAD moved aside git answers `fatal: not a git repository` — the state
that makes the filesystem fallback run — so the structural rule cannot classify
it either. The config and its credential were indexed. The read is os.Stat now,
matching git's stat(); a dangling link and a link to a non-gitfile still name
nothing, exactly as git names nothing for them. gitCommonDir keeps its lstat,
where git's own file_exists() is an lstat and a dangling `commondir` makes git
REFUSE the directory rather than ignore the file.

A `.git` pointer inside a vendored or installed-dependency tree. The sweep and
the fallback walk both pruned those trees before reading anything in them, on
the premise that nothing in them is indexed. The premise is false: a pointer's
target is somewhere else. `vendor/dep/.git` -> `gitdir: ../../.dep-git` names a
root-level git directory that is not vendored, that git lists in full, and whose
missing HEAD puts it out of every other rule's reach:

    $ git ls-files --cached --others --exclude-standard
    .dep-git/config
    pkg/source.go
    tracked.go
    $ git ls-files --cached --others --exclude-standard --directory
    .dep-git/
    pkg/
    vendor/
    tracked.go

`vendor/dep/` is in neither listing. The sweep no longer prunes on a vendored
name, and the walk reads that tree's directories — directories only, no files —
on its way out. Ignored trees are still unread, and the walk now consults the
ignore rules before the vendored name so that stays true there too; both were
already SkipDir, so the set of walked files is unchanged.

Measured, cold `search --profile syntax-only`, 3 runs after a warm-up, on a
6,268-directory repository (500 tracked source packages, an ignored
2,200-directory build tree, a 3,300-directory node_modules):

    node_modules ignored (the ordinary case)   before 0.22 0.25 0.27
                                               after  0.24 0.21 0.21
    node_modules untracked and NOT ignored     before 0.48 0.41 0.41
                                               after  0.54 0.55 0.58

The claim that a vendored tree could be skipped "since nothing in it is indexed
for a pointer there to leak through" is struck where it stood.","messageHeadline":"fix(sem): read a `.git` gitfile through a symlink, and sweep vendored…","oid":"db0f0ddaf85df8acf4da9f72c93271c4a829c774"},{"authoredDate":"2026-08-19T23:22:24Z","authors":[{"email":"257360244+suhaanthayyil@users.noreply.github.com","id":"U_kgDOD1cBdA","login":"suhaanthayyil","name":"Suhaan Thayyil"}],"committedDate":"2026-08-22T09:48:10Z","messageBody":"Git reads a gitfile into a NUL-terminated buffer and hands `buf + 8` on as a C
string, so the first NUL ends the target and the rest of the line is neither
part of the path nor an error. Keeping the NUL and its suffix produced a name
nothing on disk is called: the structure test could not find the directory, no
target was recorded, and the `--separate-git-dir` target the pointer named was
indexed with its config and hooks.

Verified on git 2.54.0:

    $ printf 'gitdir: .repo-git\0junkjunk\n' > .git
    $ git rev-parse --git-dir
    <worktree>/.repo-git
    $ git ls-files --cached --others --exclude-standard --directory
    .repo-git/
    tracked.go
    $ printf 'gitdir: \0.repo-git\n' > .git
    $ git rev-parse --git-dir
    fatal: not a git repository: (null)      (exit 128)

so the suffix is dropped, a NUL straight after the prefix is an absent target,
and a trailing space ahead of a NUL still belongs to the name. The truncation is
applied after the newline trim, which is the order git's own buffer produces.

Both consumers of the pointer -- the excluder and gitInfoExcludePath -- read it
through this one parser, so the fix closes the class. Before it, the filesystem
fallback did not merely leak: the NUL reached os.Stat and the whole search
failed with `read ignore file ...: invalid argument`.","messageHeadline":"fix(sem): stop a `.git` pointer's target at the first NUL byte","oid":"83be37f2cb4fa5be8b41a72496cc747d68537aec"},{"authoredDate":"2026-08-19T23:22:24Z","authors":[{"email":"257360244+suhaanthayyil@users.noreply.github.com","id":"U_kgDOD1cBdA","login":"suhaanthayyil","name":"Suhaan Thayyil"}],"committedDate":"2026-08-22T09:48:43Z","messageBody":"…aths

A `.git` pointer inside a tree the project's own ignore rules cover names a git
directory OUTSIDE that tree, which git lists as ordinary untracked content. Both
listing paths stopped at the ignored tree before reading anything in it, so a
committed `build/` ignore hid `build/dep/.git` -> `gitdir: ../../.dep-git` and
the root-level, HEAD-damaged git directory it names was indexed with its config
and hooks. `.gitignore` is committed content in the repository being scanned, so
pruning by it handed that repository the choice of which pointers this rule may
read -- the same reason both halves of the rule are otherwise unconditional.

Verified on git 2.54.0 with `build/` ignored and holding the pointer:

    $ git ls-files --cached --others --exclude-standard
    .dep-git/config
    pkg/source.go
    .gitignore
    tracked.go
    $ git ls-files --cached --others --exclude-standard --directory
    .dep-git/
    pkg/
    .gitignore
    tracked.go
    $ git ls-files --others --ignored --exclude-standard --directory
    build/

`build/` is in neither listing the sweep read, so no chain and no collapsed root
reaches the pointer; the third listing is the one that names it. So the sweep
asks git for the ignored roots too, drops the ignore rules from its pruning
decision, and the filesystem fallback reads an ignored tree's directories on its
way out exactly as it already does for a vendored one.

Two claims that were false when written are struck in place: that the give-up
was a narrow disclosure, and that the filesystem fallback was unaffected by it.

The price is measured, not hidden. Cold `search --profile syntax-only`, cache
directory removed before each run, on a 6,350-directory repository with 500
tracked source packages, an ignored 2,200-directory build tree and an ignored
3,300-directory node_modules (first run of each set discarded as warm-up):

    before  0.18 0.18 0.18
    after   0.50 0.51 0.50

That is one ReadDir per ignored directory and no file read at all; nothing in an
ignored tree becomes indexable, and a repository with no ignored untracked trees
pays nothing.","messageHeadline":"fix(sem): sweep an ignored tree for `.git` pointers on both listing p…","oid":"fd2ab88ed0a4663ac302575ff941e4d01dac8b96"},{"authoredDate":"2026-08-19T23:39:50Z","authors":[{"email":"suhaanthayyil0@gmail.com","id":"U_kgDOD1cBdA","login":"suhaanthayyil","name":"Suhaan Thayyil"}],"committedDate":"2026-08-22T09:49:00Z","messageBody":"Git concatenates a relative `gitdir:` or `commondir` target onto the
directory that held the file and hands the result to the OS, which walks
the components in order, so a `..` following a SYMLINK component steps
out of the LINK'S TARGET. filepath.Join cleans `..` lexically, before any
link is consulted, and named a different directory.

Verified on git 2.54.0 with `nested/link -> sub/child`:

	$ printf 'gitdir: link/../.real-git\n' > nested/.git
	$ cd nested && git rev-parse --absolute-git-dir
	<repo>/nested/sub/.real-git

and, with `adm/link -> sub/child`:

	$ printf 'link/../.common\n' > adm/commondir
	$ git --git-dir=adm rev-parse --git-common-dir
	<tmp>/adm/sub/.common

Both lexical answers name nothing on disk. On the pointer that meant no
target was recorded at all, and the HEAD-less git directory git really
names was indexed with its credentialed config; on `commondir` it called
a linked worktree's administrative directory ordinary content.

The previously disclosed give-up named only gitCommonDir. The sibling in
gitDirPointerTarget was the one that leaked, and both now go through one
sink, gitJoinRelative, which consults the filesystem only for a target
that actually carries a `..` element.

Also: gitSweepRoots now reports "git answered" only when BOTH `--directory`
listings did. On the first alone the flag went true while the ignored roots
were silently missing, so the sweep skipped the whole-tree fallback it
exists for and a pointer under an ignored tree went unread.","messageHeadline":"fix(sem): join a pointer's relative target the way git joins it","oid":"233acf3718788d04db997213d5494b433598e4f8"},{"authoredDate":"2026-08-20T00:10:16Z","authors":[{"email":"257360244+suhaanthayyil@users.noreply.github.com","id":"U_kgDOD1cBdA","login":"suhaanthayyil","name":"Suhaan Thayyil"}],"committedDate":"2026-08-22T09:50:26Z","messageBody":"…ot outside

Round 11 raised three findings, and they are one mistake made once: the NUL
rule shipped last round went into the `.git` gitfile parser, while git applies
one rule to BOTH pointer files and applies it to the bytes it read, not to the
file it found.

There are three readers of those two files now no more: `readGitPointerFile` is
the only one, and `gitPointerPath` is the only place git's rule lives. The rule
is git's own two steps — strip trailing `\r\n` off the raw buffer, then stop at
the first NUL, because git hands the buffer on as a C string — and the bound is
on the READ, never on the file.

- `commondir` had no NUL rule, so `../common\0junk` was looked up verbatim,
  objects/ and refs/ were missed, and BOTH rules called a linked worktree's
  administrative git directory ordinary content.
- The pointer's size test ran BEFORE the truncation, so a 8 KiB `.git` file
  whose target ends at byte 20 was refused — git follows it up to 1 MiB — and
  with the target's HEAD damaged that pointer was the only evidence naming it.
- `commondir` had a 4 KiB whole-file bound of its own; git has none at all.
- A `commondir` git READS and finds empty resolves to the git directory itself
  and git accepts the directory; only a file git gets nothing out of makes it
  die. Folding those together refused a git directory git accepts.
- `gitInfoExcludePath` read both files with rules of its own — a whole-file size
  test, TrimSpace, no NUL rule, a lexical join — and now reads through the same
  reader.

`TestGitPointerFilesAreReadThroughOneReader` fails if a function grows its own
reader again: naming `.git`, `gitdir: ` or `commondir` and reading a file
directly is the shape of the bypass, and on the parent commit it names all
three offenders.

Separately, `containedRel` called the repository ROOT "outside the repository",
so `gitdir: .` — which git follows to the root, then lists the git directory's
own `config` as ordinary content — recorded no target at all. The root is now a
target, and `recordTarget` is the one place it is handled: excluding the root as
a prefix would delete the caller's whole snapshot, so the git directory's own
top-level entries are excluded instead, from git's own `common_list[]` and the
per-git-directory files. `src/app.go` stays indexed; `config` does not.

Every want comes from git 2.54.0 run as an oracle, transcripts in the code.","messageHeadline":"fix(sem): one byte rule for both git pointer files, and the root is n…","oid":"69bcd7bdd904c2f534c6beba6038219a604d2c8d"},{"authoredDate":"2026-08-20T00:32:09Z","authors":[{"email":"suhaanthayyil0@gmail.com","id":"U_kgDOD1cBdA","login":"suhaanthayyil","name":"Suhaan Thayyil"}],"committedDate":"2026-08-22T09:50:27Z","messageBody":"…ist misses

A `.git` pointer naming the repository ROOT makes the git directory and the
worktree one directory, and `gitDirRootEntryNames` is the only thing separating
them. It was written from one reading of git's `path.c`, so it had never heard
of `reftable/` — where a repository initialized with `--ref-format=reftable`
keeps the ref records AND the reflogs that the loose layout keeps in `refs/`,
`packed-refs` and `logs/`, all three of which the list already excluded.

Fifteen more names were missing with it. They come from an oracle rather than
another reading: the new test drives the real git binary through the operations
that park state in a git directory and fails naming every top-level entry the
list does not cover, so the class is locked rather than one instance patched.","messageHeadline":"fix(sem): exclude the reftable ref store, and ask git what else the l…","oid":"6e5b226efffa8bf7187aafc64abd2eb961130116"},{"authoredDate":"2026-08-20T00:35:01Z","authors":[{"email":"suhaanthayyil0@gmail.com","id":"U_kgDOD1cBdA","login":"suhaanthayyil","name":"Suhaan Thayyil"}],"committedDate":"2026-08-22T09:50:27Z","messageBody":"","messageHeadline":"docs(sem): state the git version the reftable layout was verified on","oid":"fc3943b5883ddf7cabc0aa93d7a28c4c0d83c84e"},{"authoredDate":"2026-08-20T01:16:47Z","authors":[{"email":"257360244+suhaanthayyil@users.noreply.github.com","id":"U_kgDOD1cBdA","login":"suhaanthayyil","name":"Suhaan Thayyil"}],"committedDate":"2026-08-22T09:51:34Z","messageBody":"…arch

A `.git` pointer this process may not read is not "no pointer". The sweep
skipped a directory it could not `ReadDir`, and `gitDirPointerTarget` treated an
unreadable `.git` FILE as not-a-gitfile, so the git directory the pointer named
— which sits somewhere ELSE in the tree, where git lists it as ordinary
untracked content — was indexed with its credentialed config. Reproduced at run
time with the real `search` verb on both listing paths and on both shapes.

Neither remedy the report named is shippable. Propagating the error makes a
repository holding one root-owned build directory wholly unsearchable, and that
is measured rather than argued: the filesystem fallback already propagated, and
`search` over a directory with one mode-000 subdirectory answered `permission
denied` and indexed nothing. Excluding the unreadable subtree excludes the wrong
path, since the target is elsewhere by construction.

So the evidence is dropped instead of the availability. The pointer rule accepts
a target on exactly one test — `hasGitDirStructure`, objects/ and refs/ through
commondir, git's HEAD test dropped — so the directories an unread pointer could
have named are a subset of the directories carrying that structure. When, and
only when, a read failed, every observed directory carrying it becomes a target.
Nothing the readable sweep would have caught is left behind, because the
acceptance test is the same test.

The cost is one subtree, and only where evidence was hidden: a directory holding
an `objects/` and a `refs/` directory that no pointer names — `testdata/parser`
— is given up. Measured on this repository, worktree snapshot, `syntax-only`:
441 files with such a directory planted and everything readable, 440 with one
mode-000 directory beside it; 440 either way without it. Paired cold `search`,
randomized order, n=20: median -3.1 ms, 95% CI [-14.2, +26.8] ms.

walkWorktreeFiles now walks on past a directory it cannot read instead of
returning the error, which is the outage above; the sweep records the failure and
the promotion fails closed for it.","messageHeadline":"fix(sem): an unreadable pointer narrows one subtree, not the whole se…","oid":"3475ab27e3fba2ba963157ea7ad5f810f00c2f80"},{"authoredDate":"2026-08-20T01:44:40Z","authors":[{"email":"257360244+suhaanthayyil@users.noreply.github.com","id":"U_kgDOD1cBdA","login":"suhaanthayyil","name":"Suhaan Thayyil"}],"committedDate":"2026-08-22T09:51:34Z","messageBody":"The sweep's last pruning reason was "this path is already excluded", and it
had the same defect as the two reasons removed before it: an exclusion says
do not INDEX this tree, and the sweep indexes nothing. What it reads there is
a `.git` pointer, and a pointer's target is somewhere ELSE.

`vendorgit/` carries HEAD, objects/ and refs/, so the structural half of
rule 2 excludes it on sight; `vendorgit/dep/.git` -> `gitdir: ../../.dep-git`
then names a HEAD-damaged git directory at the repository root that git lists
in full and that no other rule can classify. Refusing to look inside the
excluded tree published `.dep-git/config` and the credential in it, on the
git-listing path and on the filesystem fallback alike.

The sweep now prunes on nothing, and the filesystem fallback reads the
directories of a tree it is about to SkipDir, the way it already does for a
vendored or ignored one.","messageHeadline":"fix(sem): an excluded tree is not a reason to leave its pointers unread","oid":"8595109f24621802f31d6b610d3aca8da77c39b2"},{"authoredDate":"2026-08-20T02:15:41Z","authors":[{"email":"257360244+suhaanthayyil@users.noreply.github.com","id":"U_kgDOD1cBdA","login":"suhaanthayyil","name":"Suhaan Thayyil"}],"committedDate":"2026-08-22T09:54:53Z","messageBody":"The sweep prunes on nothing, and that is still right: every prune tried
here — a vendored NAME, the project's own ignore rules, "this path is
already excluded" — is something the scanned repository can arrange, and
each one bought a hiding place for a `.git` pointer whose target sits
elsewhere in the tree and is indexed in full. But an unpruned sweep is
bounded by nothing, and its size is set by content git OMITS: it descends
every root git collapsed, ignored trees included, so a `node_modules`, a
package store or a build cache is traversed in full on every query.

Measured before this change with 2 indexed files and 110,120 directories
under an ignored `node_modules/`: one working-tree listing took 2.31-2.39 s
against 9-11 ms on main, and one cold `search` 7.06-7.23 s against 0.07 s.
Linear at ~21 us per directory, so a tree ten times that size — an ordinary
monorepo — is a minute-long query, repeated for every query.

The bound is not a fourth prune. A prune says "there is nothing to find in
here" and is wrong; a spent ledger says "I did not look, and I am not
pretending I did". Exhaustion records hidden evidence, which is what
promoteUnverifiedGitDirs already acts on: every observed directory carrying
a git directory's structure becomes an exclusion target. The pointer rule
accepts a target on exactly that test, so the directories an UNREAD pointer
could have named are a subset of the ones promotion excludes. Running the
ledger out costs the repository 20,000 real directories on disk and buys a
strictly wider exclusion, not a hiding place.

One ledger for the whole listing — every collapsed root, every ignored
root, every observePrunedSubtree call on the filesystem fallback, and the
derived-roots branch git could not answer for — so splitting one large
ignored tree into a hundred wins no fresh allowance. It is charged at
admission rather than at ReadDir, because a directory costs one ReadDir to
enumerate and one observe() per subdirectory it turns up: charged at the
read, a 20,000-read budget still let the sweep observe 110,101 directories.
The derived-roots branch now sorts its roots, since with a ledger in play
which directories the sweep reached is part of the answer and ranging a map
made that differ between runs.

The sweep also observes the caller's context now, and a cancelled query
stops it the same fail-closed way.

Four gaps in the git-directory excluder's fail-closed sweep:

- observePrunedSubtree seeded descendObserving's queue with its root
  directly, skipping the admitSweepDirectory charge every other queued
  directory pays. An exhausted ledger still paid for one uncharged ReadDir
  per pruned root, unboundedly.
- The .git gitfile reader accepted any file with a NUL inside its 4 KiB
  read window regardless of the file's real size, while git refuses any
  .git file over 1 MiB outright (a stat check, independent of NUL
  position). A multi-megabyte gitfile with an early NUL was therefore
  treated as a valid pointer when git would refuse to read it at all.
- The same reader rejected legitimate pointers whose target didn't
  terminate inside that same 4 KiB window, even though git reads and
  follows anything up to its real 1 MiB ceiling.
- gitDirRootEntryNames, used when a pointer names the repository root,
  was missing git's transient lock siblings (config.lock, index.lock,
  HEAD.lock, packed-refs.lock, shallow.lock) that a crashed git process
  can leave behind holding the file they were about to replace.

Fixes: charge the pruned-subtree root to the sweep ledger before
descending; give the gitfile reader its own maxGitFileBytes (1 MiB, git's
own ceiling) checked by stat before any byte is read, while leaving
commondir's unbounded-by-git read window untouched; add the lock names to
the root-entry allowlist.

The .git-pointer sweep's ReadDir failure only incremented hiddenEvidence,
which makes promoteUnverifiedGitDirs fail closed by excluding
structurally-git-shaped directories it can no longer rule out -- but
sweepStop stayed sweepRanToCompletion for this case, so sweepWarnings never
disclosed it. Added a sampled sweepUnreadableDirs list and a
W_GITDIR_SWEEP_UNREADABLE_DIRECTORY warning surfaced from both listing paths.

hasObjectsAndRefs called os.Stat directly on objects/refs with no volume
check, so a committed objects/refs symlink to a UNC share would dial SMB
with ambient credentials -- this probe runs over every directory the sweep
observes, not just pointer targets already guarded elsewhere. Now Lstat's
first and rejects a cross-volume symlink target before Stat follows it.

gitInfoExcludePath (ignore.go) has its own independent commondir reader with
no volume guard at all, unlike gitCommonDir in provider.go -- a linked
worktree's commondir naming a UNC share reached the caller's
os.Stat(info/exclude) unchecked. Added the same volume-name guard.

Three findings from the latest re-review:

- gitDirPointerTarget accepted a `.git` pointer's target on lexical
  containment alone (a plain string comparison) before ever resolving
  symlinks. A target that LOOKS like it is inside the repository
  (`admin-link`) but is itself a symlink or junction to an external or
  network-backed directory was reported as contained, letting
  hasGitDirStructure probe commondir/objects/refs through that link.
  Every target now goes through the same EvalSymlinks-based resolution
  the "escaping the worktree" case already used, falling back to the
  lexical answer only when the target does not exist at all (nothing
  on disk for a symlink to redirect).

- hasObjectsAndRefs' volume comparison read a RELATIVE symlink target
  from os.Readlink and compared its (always-empty, for a relative
  path) volume directly against the repository's absolute volume,
  rejecting every relative objects/refs symlink on Windows -- a layout
  git itself accepts. Relative targets are now resolved against the
  entry's own parent before the volume comparison, via the same
  gitJoinRelative helper already used for `.git`/`commondir` pointers.

- promoteUnverifiedGitDirs never considered the repository root a
  candidate, parroting observe()'s (differently-motivated) root
  exemption for direct invocation on a bare repo. A hidden `.git`
  pointer that would have named the root -- root itself holding
  objects/ and refs/ at its top level -- fell through the one gap
  promotion left uncovered, even though a READ pointer naming the root
  already narrows to root's own git-owned entries via
  recordGitDirRootEntries rather than excluding the whole worktree.
  Root is now probed the same way, gated behind the same
  hiddenEvidence condition that keeps an ordinary bare-repo scan
  untouched.

Three findings from re-review:

- ListIgnoredWorktreeDirectoryEntries returned every individual filename
  when a directory was ignored only by file-pattern rules mixed with other
  content (git's --directory flag cannot collapse it in that case), so a
  large pattern-ignored build/cache tree could return hundreds of
  thousands of entries before the sweep's 20,000-directory budget ever
  applied. Filter to actual directory entries (trailing slash) during the
  NUL split itself, matching what the only consumer already required.

- The sharedindex.<hash> root-entry matcher accepted any name with that
  bare prefix, so legitimate source like sharedindex.go was silently
  excluded whenever a pointer made the repository root double as its own
  git directory. Validate the suffix is 40 or 64 lowercase hex characters,
  matching what git update-index --split-index actually writes.

- gitDirPointerTarget read the .git file with a bare os.Stat, which
  follows a symlink as part of the same syscall that reports its result.
  A .git that is itself a symlink to a UNC path would dial SMB with
  ambient credentials before the function ever got to inspect the target.
  Lstat first and reject a cross-volume link target before any Stat
  follows it, the same pattern already used for objects/refs entries.

Windows volume names are case-insensitive but filepath.VolumeName preserves
spelling, so raw != comparisons falsely rejected same-volume paths spelled
differently (C: vs c:). Added sameVolume (strings.EqualFold) and applied it
everywhere a volume is compared in provider.go.

hasObjectsAndRefs, gitDirPointerTarget, and gitCommonDir only checked the
first hop of a symlink/junction chain before stat-ing objects/refs or a
gitdir/commondir file. A chain that only left the volume on a later hop
(local -> local -> UNC) bypassed the check and reached the network. Added
safeStatThroughSymlinks to resolve hop-by-hop with a volume check at each
step and a hop ceiling, and switched all three call sites to it.

config.worktree.lock (lockfile.c's sibling of config.worktree, git 2.46+)
was missing from gitDirRootEntryNames, so a root git-dir exception could
leave a live worktree-config rewrite indexed as source, credentials
included.

Adds regression tests: multi-hop same-volume chains still resolve, chains
past the hop ceiling are refused, and config.worktree.lock is excluded at
a root git dir.

ListIgnoredWorktreeDirectoryEntries went through run(), which materializes
the complete `git ls-files --others --ignored --directory` stdout into a
bytes.Buffer (and then a string) before splitNULDirectoryEntries ever
discarded a non-directory field. A directory ignored only by a
file-pattern rule (e.g. *.o) alongside other content is never collapsed
by --directory, so an attacker-controlled checkout with such a tree makes
git print every one of those filenames individually, all buffered in full
before the first byte is filtered. streamNULDirectoryEntries now reads the
subprocess stdout through a pipe and filters each NUL-delimited field as
it arrives, so cost tracks the number of ignored/untracked directories
(the only quantity any caller uses) rather than every ignored file.

gitInfoExcludePath compared commondir's volume against gitDir's with a raw
!=, so a commondir spelled with a lowercase drive letter ("c:") while
gitDir carried an uppercase one ("C:") was rejected as a different volume
even though Windows treats them identically — silently skipping the
shared info/exclude file. Switched to the existing case-insensitive
sameVolume helper, matching every other volume comparison in this package.

gitDirLinkTarget (the "`.git` is a symlink to a directory" case) read the
link's target with a bare os.Stat, which resolves the whole symlink chain
— including an off-volume hop — in the same syscall that reports the
result. A `.git` symlinked to a UNC directory would dial SMB with ambient
credentials before this function ever got to look at, let alone reject,
the target, unlike the sibling gitfile-pointer case which already guards
this through safeStatThroughSymlinks. Applied the same guard here.

git ls-files --ignored --directory never collapses a directory ignored
only by a file-pattern rule (*.o, node_modules/*.log), so a repository
that arranges for millions of such matches and zero collapsible
directories made streamNULDirectoryEntries read and discard every one of
them before the sweep's own directory budget ever applied. Cap the total
fields read (maxIgnoredDirectoryFields) and report the listing truncated
past it; the caller already treats a failed listing as a reason to fall
back to its own budgeted derivation.

ignore.go's info/exclude resolver reimplemented commondir parsing inline
with only a single-hop volume check, instead of reusing gitCommonDir
(provider.go), which already walks a commondir symlink hop by hop via
safeStatThroughSymlinks before opening it. A commondir that was itself a
same-volume local symlink to a second symlink naming a UNC share could
dial SMB with ambient credentials through the path this function never
even looked at. Route it through the shared, already-audited resolver
instead of a second hand-rolled one.

Also widen maxGitPointerBytes from 4 KiB to 64 KiB: git puts no size
limit on commondir and concatenates its lexical text without collapsing
it, so a legitimate pointer padded by repeated ./ components could
exceed the old window with no NUL to signal an early stop, refusing a
real linked worktree's git directory instead of excluding it.

already set, and the repository under analysis controls which of them runs.

provider.go:9782 sets batch.SetMaxBytes(maxReadBytes) and provider.go:9785
then handed any path containing a newline to the unbounded gitutil.ShowFile.
The batch protocol is line based, so that fallback is real -- but it is
selected by the file's NAME, so a repository could opt one blob out of the
cap by naming it. Measured on a 64 MiB file named "a\nb.py" (packed .git
400 KB), `entire graph symbols`: 0.35 s / 21 MB when the same file is named
plain.py, 28.9 s / 2.53 GB with the newline. search.go:1434 had the same
fallback under batch.SetMaxBytes(defaultMaxParseBytes).

analyze.go:109 and :115 read BOTH sides of every changed file with no cap and
no newline needed, so one large blob set the whole command's cost: on a
20 MB .go file `entire graph commit` took 13.5 s / 2.55 GB.

All four now read through gitutil.ShowFileLimited (git.go:566), which probes
the blob size and refuses before allocating -- the contract callsite.go:126
already relies on. The diff cap is maxDiffFileBytes = defaultMaxParseBytes:
a file the snapshot declines to parse is not one the diff should read twice
in order to parse anyway (on that fixture the dependents scan was already
reporting big.go as E_FILE_TOO_LARGE). After: symbols 0.08 s / 21 MB,
commit 0.09 s / 32 MB.

A refused file is reported, not dropped silently. The diff emits an
E_FILE_TOO_LARGE warning naming the side that was refused, reusing the
provider's code as dependents.go:275 already does; the snapshot routes the
refusal through its existing partial-failure path.

One behaviour change is deliberate and visible: an oversized blob whose path
contains a newline can no longer produce a file record, because its size,
hash and line count were previously learned by reading it. At HEAD it now
reports E_FILE_READ instead of E_FILE_TOO_LARGE and completeness moves to
degraded -- which is the truthful state for a file the graph skipped without
being able to measure it. Restoring the record needs the refused size from

could not read, dropped the FileRecord, and turned a warning-severity
E_FILE_TOO_LARGE into an error-severity E_FILE_READ. Completeness fell from
ok to unsafe and the file was gone because of how it was NAMED.

ProviderSnapshotOptions.MaxParseBytes documents the opposite: an oversized
file still emits a file record and a partial failure, with the record's blob
hash and line count coming from a streamed digest. The batch reader keeps
that promise for every path it can carry; the fallback now keeps it too.

gitutil.OversizeBlobAtRev is the companion ShowFileLimited owed its callers:
it streams the blob past a digest and discards it, reporting the same
OversizeBlob the batch reader records, with the bytes never held. Its
"found" return means "exists AND is over the ceiling", so a read that failed
for any other reason cannot be recorded as too large. fallbackOversizeRegistry
notes the refused paths and resolves each at most once, deferred until a
caller asks, mirroring the working-tree oversizeRegistry beside it.

  after this     0.21 s    20 MB   files=2  E_FILE_TOO_LARGE  completeness=ok

process launched afterward, so terminateAndWait could kill or wait on

ls-tree -l's per-blob size lookup (and every other Git subprocess this
package runs) can silently contact a promisor remote to fetch a missing
object in a partial clone, violating the provider's no-egress contract.
Disable lazy fetching for every Git command; ls-tree -l already reports an
unfetchable blob via its BAD size sentinel, which callers already classify
as LimitedFileUnreadable rather than an error.

buildReferenceIndex's oversize-file warning relied on oversizeMatched, which
is only ever populated by the batch reader's content scanner. A candidate
whose path that reader rejects (line-unsafe) or that reader never started at
all falls back to LimitedFileReader, which cannot scan content, so
oversizeMatched stayed false forever for it -- silently dropping
E_FILE_TOO_LARGE on the full-tree fallback even when the file does contain a
changed name. The adjacent unaddressable-path warning had the same gap,
gated on prefiltered even though an unaddressable path never has content
evidence either way. Both now warn when there is no candidate evidence to
rule a path out, rather than assuming a miss.

Prime's ordinary short-path metadata batches ran to completion regardless
of SetDeadline, so a long fallback candidate list could keep starting new
Git subprocesses well past the caller's wall-clock budget. Check the
deadline between batches and mark the remainder unaddressable once it
elapses, same as the existing component-by-component traversal.

Separately, an oversized committed file with no extension can only be
classified by its shebang line, but Git blob reads are all-or-nothing, so
the bounded prefix read that shebang routing needs was impossible on an
oversized blob and the file silently vanished (no file record, no partial
failure) before the oversize registry was ever consulted. Capture a
leading prefix for free during the digest streaming pass every oversized
blob already pays for, on both the batch reader and the newline-fallback
path, and route by it instead of retrying a read that is guaranteed to
fail the same way.

GIT_NO_LAZY_FETCH is silently ignored and a partial clone's promisor
remote would still be lazily fetched with no guard active at all.
GIT_ALLOW_PROTOCOL has gated every transport since Git 2.11.1; set to
empty on every git subprocess, it denies fetch/clone/push over every
protocol regardless of Git version, closing the gap independently of
whether the lazy-fetch guard itself is recognized.

A review finding claimed blobSizeAtRev's already-root-relative treePath gets
the subdirectory prefix reapplied by ls-tree because treeEntryMetadataBatch
runs with repo as cwd (e.g. "scope/scope/file"), causing ReadFileLimited's
size probe to miss and fall back to materializing oversized blobs whole.

Verified independently with a bare `git ls-tree ... :(top,literal)path`
invocation from a subdirectory cwd: the `top` pathspec magic anchors a
literal pathspec to the repository root regardless of cwd, so no double
prefix occurs. Two existing tests already cover this scenario for ordinary
content reads and passed unmodified. This adds the adversarial case the
finding specifically raised -- an oversized blob probed from a subdirectory
repo, both one and two path components deep -- and asserts the probe itself
succeeds (LimitedFileOversize with the exact size, no content read) rather
than falling through to the unbounded git-show path. It passes against the
unmodified code, so the finding is dismissed as a false positive rather than
changed.

gitInfoExcludePath compared commondir's volume against gitDir's with a raw
!=, so a commondir spelled with a lowercase drive letter ("c:") while
gitDir carried an uppercase one ("C:") was rejected as a different volume
even though Windows treats them identically — silently skipping the
shared info/exclude file. Switched to the existing case-insensitive
sameVolume helper, matching every other volume comparison in this package.

gitDirLinkTarget (the "`.git` is a symlink to a directory" case) read the
link's target with a bare os.Stat, which resolves the whole symlink chain
— including an off-volume hop — in the same syscall that reports the
result. A `.git` symlinked to a UNC directory would dial SMB with ambient
credentials before this function ever got to look at, let alone reject,
the target, unlike the sibling gitfile-pointer case which already guards
this through safeStatThroughSymlinks. Applied the same guard here.

git ls-files --ignored --directory never collapses a directory ignored
only by a file-pattern rule (*.o, node_modules/*.log), so a repository
that arranges for millions of such matches and zero collapsible
directories made streamNULDirectoryEntries read and discard every one of
them before the sweep's own directory budget ever applied. Cap the total
fields read (maxIgnoredDirectoryFields) and report the listing truncated
past it; the caller already treats a failed listing as a reason to fall
back to its own budgeted derivation.

ignore.go's info/exclude resolver reimplemented commondir parsing inline
with only a single-hop volume check, instead of reusing gitCommonDir
(provider.go), which already walks a commondir symlink hop by hop via
safeStatThroughSymlinks before opening it. A commondir that was itself a
same-volume local symlink to a second symlink naming a UNC share could
dial SMB with ambient credentials through the path this function never
even looked at. Route it through the shared, already-audited resolver
instead of a second hand-rolled one.

Also widen maxGitPointerBytes from 4 KiB to 64 KiB: git puts no size
limit on commondir and concatenates its lexical text without collapsing
it, so a legitimate pointer padded by repeated ./ components could
exceed the old window with no NUL to signal an early stop, refusing a
real linked worktree's git directory instead of excluding it.

ls-tree -l's per-blob size lookup (and every other Git subprocess this
package runs) can silently contact a promisor remote to fetch a missing
object in a partial clone, violating the provider's no-egress contract.
Disable lazy fetching for every Git command; ls-tree -l already reports an
unfetchable blob via its BAD size sentinel, which callers already classify
as LimitedFileUnreadable rather than an error.

buildReferenceIndex's oversize-file warning relied on oversizeMatched, which
is only ever populated by the batch reader's content scanner. A candidate
whose path that reader rejects (line-unsafe) or that reader never started at
all falls back to LimitedFileReader, which cannot scan content, so
oversizeMatched stayed false forever for it -- silently dropping
E_FILE_TOO_LARGE on the full-tree fallback even when the file does contain a
changed name. The adjacent unaddressable-path warning had the same gap,
gated on prefiltered even though an unaddressable path never has content
evidence either way. Both now warn when there is no candidate evidence to
rule a path out, rather than assuming a miss.

Prime's ordinary short-path metadata batches ran to completion regardless
of SetDeadline, so a long fallback candidate list could keep starting new
Git subprocesses well past the caller's wall-clock budget. Check the
deadline between batches and mark the remainder unaddressable once it
elapses, same as the existing component-by-component traversal.

Separately, an oversized committed file with no extension can only be
classified by its shebang line, but Git blob reads are all-or-nothing, so
the bounded prefix read that shebang routing needs was impossible on an
oversized blob and the file silently vanished (no file record, no partial
failure) before the oversize registry was ever consulted. Capture a
leading prefix for free during the digest streaming pass every oversized
blob already pays for, on both the batch reader and the newline-fallback
path, and route by it instead of retrying a read that is guaranteed to
fail the same way.

remote would still be lazily fetched with no guard active at all.
GIT_ALLOW_PROTOCOL has gated every transport since Git 2.11.1; set to
empty on every git subprocess, it denies fetch/clone/push over every
protocol regardless of Git version, closing the gap independently of
whether the lazy-fetch guard itself is recognized.

A review finding claimed blobSizeAtRev's already-root-relative treePath gets
the subdirectory prefix reapplied by ls-tree because treeEntryMetadataBatch
runs with repo as cwd (e.g. "scope/scope/file"), causing ReadFileLimited's
size probe to miss and fall back to materializing oversized blobs whole.

Verified independently with a bare `git ls-tree ... :(top,literal)path`
invocation from a subdirectory cwd: the `top` pathspec magic anchors a
literal pathspec to the repository root regardless of cwd, so no double
prefix occurs. Two existing tests already cover this scenario for ordinary
content reads and passed unmodified. This adds the adversarial case the
finding specifically raised -- an oversized blob probed from a subdirectory
repo, both one and two path components deep -- and asserts the probe itself
succeeds (LimitedFileOversize with the exact size, no content read) rather
than falling through to the unbounded git-show path. It passes against the
unmodified code, so the finding is dismissed as a false positive rather than
changed.

gitInfoExcludePath compared commondir's volume against gitDir's with a raw
!=, so a commondir spelled with a lowercase drive letter ("c:") while
gitDir carried an uppercase one ("C:") was rejected as a different volume
even though Windows treats them identically — silently skipping the
shared info/exclude file. Switched to the existing case-insensitive
sameVolume helper, matching every other volume comparison in this package.

gitDirLinkTarget (the "`.git` is a symlink to a directory" case) read the
link's target with a bare os.Stat, which resolves the whole symlink chain
— including an off-volume hop — in the same syscall that reports the
result. A `.git` symlinked to a UNC directory would dial SMB with ambient
credentials before this function ever got to look at, let alone reject,
the target, unlike the sibling gitfile-pointer case which already guards
this through safeStatThroughSymlinks. Applied the same guard here.

git ls-files --ignored --directory never collapses a directory ignored
only by a file-pattern rule (*.o, node_modules/*.log), so a repository
that arranges for millions of such matches and zero collapsible
directories made streamNULDirectoryEntries read and discard every one of
them before the sweep's own directory budget ever applied. Cap the total
fields read (maxIgnoredDirectoryFields) and report the listing truncated
past it; the caller already treats a failed listing as a reason to fall
back to its own budgeted derivation.

ignore.go's info/exclude resolver reimplemented commondir parsing inline
with only a single-hop volume check, instead of reusing gitCommonDir
(provider.go), which already walks a commondir symlink hop by hop via
safeStatThroughSymlinks before opening it. A commondir that was itself a
same-volume local symlink to a second symlink naming a UNC share could
dial SMB with ambient credentials through the path this function never
even looked at. Route it through the shared, already-audited resolver
instead of a second hand-rolled one.

Also widen maxGitPointerBytes from 4 KiB to 64 KiB: git puts no size
limit on commondir and concatenates its lexical text without collapsing
it, so a legitimate pointer padded by repeated ./ components could
exceed the old window with no NUL to signal an early stop, refusing a
real linked worktree's git directory instead of excluding it.

# Search Checkpoints

Use `entire search` to find relevant checkpoints before guessing from memory.

## Response Format

Begin the first response to this skill invocation with the line:

`Entire Search:`

followed by a blank line, then the content.

- Apply the header to the **first response of the invocation only.** Do not re-print it on follow-up turns within the same invocation (e.g. after the user answers a clarifying question).
- Do **not** include the header on error or early-exit responses (e.g. "Entire CLI not installed", "authentication required", "no matches"). The header's presence should signal that the skill ran and produced real output.

## When to Use

- The user asks things like "have we done this before?", "search past work", "find the previous implementation", or "look for checkpoints about X"
- You need prior context from another branch, repo, author, or recent time period
- You want likely matches first, then a deeper transcript read only for the best hit

Do not use this for the current active session. Use `session-handoff` for that.

## Process

1. Run a focused search with JSON output so results are easy to inspect:

```bash
entire search "<query>" --json
```

Add filters when the user already gave them or when the first search is too broad:

```bash
entire search "<query>" --json --repo owner/name --branch branch-name --author "Name" --date week
```

Inline filters are also supported in the query: `author:<name>`, `date:<week|month>`, `branch:<name>`, `repo:<owner/name>`, `repo:*`.

2. Review the top matches and summarize the likely candidates for the user. Do not dump raw JSON unless they ask for it.

3. If the user wants details on a specific result, open the checkpoint with:

```bash
entire explain --checkpoint <checkpoint-id> --full --no-pager
```

If `--full` fails, fall back to:

```bash
entire explain --checkpoint <checkpoint-id> --raw-transcript --no-pager
```

## Search Heuristics

- Start with the user's domain terms, feature name, error text, file name, or ticket ID
- Prefer narrower searches before increasing `--limit`
- Add `--repo` or `repo:*` explicitly when repository scope matters
- If there are no useful hits, broaden in this order: remove branch filter, widen date, simplify query terms

## Failure Modes

- If search says authentication is required, tell the user to run `entire login`
- If there are no matches, say that clearly and mention the filters or query terms you tried
- If the user really wants the current session, switch to `session-handoff` instead of searching checkpoints

- If there are no matches, say that clearly and mention the filters or query terms you tried

entire checkpoint explain — Explain a session, commit, or checkpoint
Explain provides human-readable context about sessions, commits, and checkpoints.

Use this command to understand what happened during agent-driven development,
either for self-review or to understand a teammate's work.

By default, shows checkpoints on the current branch. Pass a checkpoint ID or
commit SHA as a positional argument to explain a specific item, or use flags.

Viewing specific items:
  entire checkpoint explain <id-or-sha>           Auto-detects checkpoint ID or commit SHA
  entire checkpoint explain --checkpoint <id>     Force interpretation as checkpoint ID
  entire checkpoint explain --commit <ref>        Force interpretation as commit ref

Checkpoints in another repo:
  entire checkpoint explain <id> --repo owner/name
                 Explain a checkpoint owned by another repository — the
                 drill-down for a cross-repo 'entire search' hit. Reads it from
                 that repo's Entire API; nothing is written to this repo.
                 Needs a full checkpoint ID (positional or --checkpoint) and a
                 checkpoint that has been pushed.

Filtering the list view:
  --session      Filter checkpoints by session ID (or prefix)

Output verbosity levels (when explaining a specific item):
  Default:         Detailed view with scoped prompts (ID, session, tokens, intent, prompts, files)
  --short          Summary only (ID, session, timestamp, tokens, intent)
  --full           Parsed full transcript (all prompts/responses from entire session)
  --raw-transcript Raw transcript file (JSONL format)

Machine-readable export modes (additive surface for external consumers):
  --json           Metadata-only JSON. Lists checkpoints when no target is given;
                   emits a single checkpoint envelope when a target is supplied.
                   Transcript bytes are NEVER embedded in the JSON envelope.
  --transcript     Stream stored checkpoint transcript bytes (JSONL) to stdout
                   for the selected session. Same bytes as --raw-transcript
                   while checkpoints v1 is the checkpoint store.
  --session-index  Pick a session within a multi-session checkpoint (0-based).
                   Defaults to the latest session. Only meaningful with
                   --transcript or --raw-transcript.
  --limit          Cap the number of checkpoints returned by the list view.
                   Defaults to 100. When the cap is hit, a stderr note
                   says how many were skipped. Only meaningful with --json.

Summary generation:
  --generate    Generate an AI summary for the checkpoint
  --force       Regenerate even if a summary already exists (requires --generate)

Performance options:
  --search-all  Remove branch/depth limits when searching for commits (may be slow)

Checkpoint detail view shows:
  - Author of the checkpoint
  - Associated git commits that reference the checkpoint
  - Prompts and responses from the session

Note: --session filters the list view; the positional arg, --commit, and --checkpoint are mutually exclusive.

entire api — Make an authenticated request to an Entire API and print the response
Make an authenticated HTTP request to an Entire API and print the JSON response.

These endpoints are internal and can change shape without notice; where a
purpose-built command exists, its output is the stable interface.

The CLI attaches the right bearer token and dials the right host for the
chosen backend, so you don't have to plumb auth yourself:

  --to core   the control plane (default): orgs, repos, mirrors, clusters, /me
  --to cell   your home entire-api cell: /me/* activity, repo aggregates

Use --jurisdiction <slug> (e.g. us, eu) to reach a specific jurisdiction's
entire-api cell instead of your home one; it implies --to cell.

<path> is the full path on that host, e.g. /api/v1/clusters. These
placeholders are filled from the current repo's origin remote:
  {owner} {repo}   the GitHub owner / repo
  {repo_id}        the repo's Entire ULID (from its mirror) — cells key on this

The method is GET unless a field/body is given (then POST); override with -X.

When to use this:
LAST RESORT. Right in two cases: you are developing against Entire's own
APIs and want a raw response, or no first-class command covers your need.
Otherwise prefer the command built for the job (checkpoint, session, trail,
status, repo, …) — its output is stable, raw endpoints are not. If you are
reaching for this during ordinary work in a repo with Entire enabled, run
`entire agent-help` first; there is probably a command for it. When you do
need it, use this rather than hand-rolling curl — it attaches the right
bearer and dials the right host for you.

Examples:
entire api /api/v1/clusters
  entire api --to cell /api/v1/me/activity
  entire api --jurisdiction eu /api/v1/me/activity
  entire api --to cell "/api/v1/me/recap?repo={repo_id}"
  entire api -X POST /api/v1/projects -f name=demo

Current repo: gh/entireio/entire-graph  (auto-detected from origin; pass --repo only for a DIFFERENT repo)

Flags:
  -F, --field stringArray       add a typed parameter in key=value format; true/false/null/numbers are converted (repeatable)
  -H, --header stringArray      add a request header in key:value format (repeatable)
  -i, --include                 print the response status line and headers too
      --input string            file with the request body ("-" for stdin)
  -j, --jurisdiction string     target a specific jurisdiction's cell (e.g. us, eu) instead of your home cell; implies --to cell
  -X, --method string           HTTP method (default GET, or POST when a field/body is given)
  -f, --raw-field stringArray   add a string parameter in key=value format (repeatable)
      --to string               which backend to call: core or cell (default "core")

The read-side containment in this change is fine to keep as defense in depth. The
write-side restriction is not: it breaks a supported layout to defend against an
attacker who, by the time they can exploit it, no longer needs to.

validateWritePath rejected the write when any component beneath the cache root was
a symlink. Operators symlink parts of a cache directory routinely — onto a larger
volume, into a shared cache, out of a container's writable layer — and for them
this turned `entire graph index` into a hard failure:

    $ entire graph index --repo . --head --cache-dir <dir-with-symlinked-search>
    persist preindex snapshot: cache path component ".../cache/search" is a symlink
    artifacts written: 0

Search's own writes are best effort, so they degraded quietly; preindex surfaced it
as an error. Neither is worth it. Anyone who can plant a symlink inside the cache
directory can equally write the artifact itself, so the restriction buys nothing
against a real attacker while costing a working configuration.

Reads keep the os.Root boundary. That is the side where the file's CONTENT enters
the process, and it is cheap: a cache miss is always a correct outcome, so refusing
to follow an escaping symlink costs a re-index rather than a failure.

The paths involved are cacheDir + a constant family + a constant version + a
lowercase SHA-256 hex digest, so there is no attacker-controlled component to
inject. newCacheEntry's validation of that invariant is kept because it is cheap
and makes the invariant explicit, not because it closes a live hole.

* fix(cache): confine cache reads, but stop refusing to write into a symlinked cache dir

The read-side containment in this change is fine to keep as defense in depth. The
write-side restriction is not: it breaks a supported layout to defend against an
attacker who, by the time they can exploit it, no longer needs to.

validateWritePath rejected the write when any component beneath the cache root was
a symlink. Operators symlink parts of a cache directory routinely — onto a larger
volume, into a shared cache, out of a container's writable layer — and for them
this turned `entire graph index` into a hard failure:

    $ entire graph index --repo . --head --cache-dir <dir-with-symlinked-search>
    persist preindex snapshot: cache path component ".../cache/search" is a symlink
    artifacts written: 0

Search's own writes are best effort, so they degraded quietly; preindex surfaced it
as an error. Neither is worth it. Anyone who can plant a symlink inside the cache
directory can equally write the artifact itself, so the restriction buys nothing
against a real attacker while costing a working configuration.

Reads keep the os.Root boundary. That is the side where the file's CONTENT enters
the process, and it is cheap: a cache miss is always a correct outcome, so refusing
to follow an escaping symlink costs a re-index rather than a failure.

Note for the record that the finding this PR was opened for is a false positive.
The paths involved are cacheDir + a constant family + a constant version + a
lowercase SHA-256 hex digest, so there is no attacker-controlled component to
inject. newCacheEntry's validation of that invariant is kept because it is cheap
and makes the invariant explicit, not because it closes a live hole.

TestCacheWritesTolerateSymlinkedCacheDirectories pins the asymmetry so the
restriction is not reintroduced by accident; the preindex case in
TestSearchCacheLoadersRejectSymlinkEscape now asserts that the durability READ
rejects the escape while the write succeeds.

worktreeSnapshotCacheable required a wholly pristine working tree before it
would reuse a tree-keyed index. It asked WorktreeMatchesHEAD, which is a plain
`git status --porcelain --untracked-files=all` compared against empty output, so
a single file no parser ever opens — .DS_Store, a compiled binary, a log, an
editor swap file — disabled the cache for the entire repository and every query
re-indexed from scratch.

Measured on this repo before the change: index_cache_hit=false and
index_latency_ms=9062 on a back-to-back repeat of the same search.

A path that cannot contribute a symbol or a relation cannot make a snapshot
stale, so it is not a reason to discard one. The gate now forgives exactly those
paths and nothing else:

  - gitutil gains WorktreeDirtyPaths, the factual list of diverging paths.
    WorktreeMatchesHEAD becomes len(paths)==0 and keeps its contract, so its
    existing callers and tests are unaffected. Both sides of a rename are
    reported, since porcelain -z spends a second record on the source path.
  - worktreeSnapshotCacheable forgives a dirty path only when
    extensionUnsupported says so — the same predicate the indexer uses to skip a
    file, so the two cannot disagree about what is read.

Conservative in the safe direction. An extensionless path counts as supported,
because a shebang can make it a script. Any supported path still bypasses the
cache whatever its status, and the forgiveness is per-path rather than a blanket
"ignore untracked". A .gitignore edit is forgiven, which is sound: ignore rules
can only change whether UNTRACKED files are walked, and an untracked file that
is indexable already fails the gate on its own.

Tests: WorktreeDirtyPaths over clean/untracked/modified/renamed/ignored trees,
and a snapshot-level pair asserting an unindexable untracked file keeps the cache
warm with an identical symbol set while an untracked .go file, and an
extensionless file, both still bypass it.

* fix(cache): do not forgive manifests the resolver reads, and unpin the test from the developer's global gitignore

Two problems with forgiving unindexable dirty paths, plus the comment that led to
the first.

extensionUnsupported decides whether a file is PARSED, but parsing is not the only
way a file reaches the graph. buildManifestImportResolver also reads the CONTENT of
the repo-root manifests, and two of those — go.mod and setup.cfg — carry no
supported extension while deciding how every import in the repository resolves.
Editing go.mod alone therefore kept the cache warm and served call edges still
resolved against the previous module path:

    module example.com/old -> example.com/renamed, go.mod the only dirty file
    before: Index: cache-hit   Callers: - main (main.go:5) [import_resolved]
    after:  Index: cache-miss  Callers: - none

They are now excluded by name through isManifestImportFile, listed beside the
resolver in manifestImportFiles. TestManifestImportFilesCoverReads walks
buildManifestImportResolver's AST for readContent string literals and fails if the
list falls behind, so the two cannot drift — the guarantee the doc comment claimed
but did not have. The win this change exists for is unaffected: a stray .DS_Store,
.log or .o still keeps the cache warm, and an untracked .go still bypasses it.

TestWorktreeDirtyPaths asserted that an untracked .DS_Store is reported, but
newWorktreeRepo left core.excludesFile alone, so git status honoured the
developer's global ignore. The stock macOS one lists .DS_Store — GitHub's own
gitignore guidance recommends it — making the case green on CI runners, which have
no global ignore, and red on the machine of anyone who followed that advice. The
fixture now points core.excludesFile at an empty file outside the repo, which makes
all five subtests hermetic rather than just this one.

The doc comment on worktreeSnapshotCacheable claimed extensionUnsupported was "the
same predicate the indexer uses to skip a file, so the two can never disagree about
what is read". Rewritten to say what is true, including the ignore-rule asymmetry:
git never ignores a tracked file while the provider's walk applies the ignore stack
to every path, and that disagreement can only ever report a path as dirty that the
walk would have skipped — costing a re-index, never serving a stale snapshot.

a single file no parser ever opens — .DS_Store, a compiled binary, a log, an
editor swap file — disabled the cache for the entire repository and every query
re-indexed from scratch.

Measured on this repo before the change: index_cache_hit=false and
index_latency_ms=9062 on a back-to-back repeat of the same search.

A path that cannot contribute a symbol or a relation cannot make a snapshot
stale, so it is not a reason to discard one. The gate now forgives exactly those
paths and nothing else:

    WorktreeMatchesHEAD becomes len(paths)==0 and keeps its contract, so its
    existing callers and tests are unaffected. Both sides of a rename are
    reported, since porcelain -z spends a second record on the source path.
  - worktreeSnapshotCacheable forgives a dirty path only when
    extensionUnsupported says so — the same predicate the indexer uses to skip a
    file, so the two cannot disagree about what is read.

because a shebang can make it a script. Any supported path still bypasses the
cache whatever its status, and the forgiveness is per-path rather than a blanket
"ignore untracked". A .gitignore edit is forgiven, which is sound: ignore rules
can only change whether UNTRACKED files are walked, and an untracked file that
is indexable already fails the gate on its own.

Tests: WorktreeDirtyPaths over clean/untracked/modified/renamed/ignored trees,
and a snapshot-level pair asserting an unindexable untracked file keeps the cache
warm with an identical symbol set while an untracked .go file, and an
extensionless file, both still bypass it.

the first.

extensionUnsupported decides whether a file is PARSED, but parsing is not the only
way a file reaches the graph. buildManifestImportResolver also reads the CONTENT of
the repo-root manifests, and two of those — go.mod and setup.cfg — carry no
supported extension while deciding how every import in the repository resolves.
Editing go.mod alone therefore kept the cache warm and served call edges still
resolved against the previous module path:

    module example.com/old -> example.com/renamed, go.mod the only dirty file
    before: Index: cache-hit   Callers: - main (main.go:5) [import_resolved]
    after:  Index: cache-miss  Callers: - none

but did not have. The win this change exists for is unaffected: a stray .DS_Store,
